imo-isl-2007-a2.title: Bound $f(n)\le n+1$, then constructions
imo-isl-2007-a2.body:
Let $f$ satisfy the condition.

**$f$ is nondecreasing.** For $m>n$,
$$f(m)=f\big(n+(m-n)\big)\ge f(n)+f\big(f(m-n)\big)-1\ge f(n),$$
because $f\big(f(m-n)\big)\ge1$.

**$f(n)\le n+1$ for all $n$.** If $f\equiv1$ this is clear. Otherwise let $a$ be the smallest positive integer with $f(a)>1$; by monotonicity $f(b)>1$ for all $b\ge a$.

Suppose $f(n)>n$ for some $n$. Applying the condition with $m=f(n)-n$ and $n$:
$$f\big(f(n)\big)=f\big((f(n)-n)+n\big)\ge f\big(f(n)-n\big)+f\big(f(n)\big)-1,$$
so $f\big(f(n)-n\big)\le1$, i.e. $f\big(f(n)-n\big)=1$ and therefore $f(n)-n<a$. Hence the differences $f(n)-n$ are bounded above, and among the $n$ with $f(n)>n$ (if there are any) we can pick $k$ with $c=f(k)-k\ge1$ maximal. Then $f(2k)\le 2k+c$ (either $f(2k)\le 2k$, or $f(2k)-2k\le c$ by maximality). On the other hand, since $f(k)>k$ and $f$ is nondecreasing, $f\big(f(k)\big)\ge f(k)$, so
$$2k+c\ge f(2k)=f(k+k)\ge f(k)+f\big(f(k)\big)-1\ge 2f(k)-1=2k+2c-1.$$
Thus $c\le1$, which proves $f(n)\le n+1$ for every $n$. In particular $f(2007)\le2008$.

**Every value $1,\dots,2008$ occurs.**

*Values $j=1,\dots,2007$.* Let $f_j(n)=\max\{1,\;n+j-2007\}$. Then $f_j(2007)=j$, $f_j$ is nondecreasing and $f_j(t)\le t$ for all $t$ (as $j\le2007$), so $f_j\big(f_j(n)\big)\le f_j(n)\le n$.
- If $f_j(m)=1$: $f_j(m)+f_j(f_j(n))-1=f_j(f_j(n))\le f_j(n)\le f_j(m+n)$.
- Otherwise $f_j(m)=m+j-2007$ and $f_j(m)+f_j(f_j(n))-1\le (m+j-2007)+n-1<f_j(m+n)$, since $f_j(m+n)\ge m+n+j-2007$.

*Value $2008$.* Let $g(n)=n$ if $2007\nmid n$ and $g(n)=n+1$ if $2007\mid n$; then $g(2007)=2008$ and $n\le g(n)\le n+1$. Also $g\big(g(n)\big)\le n+1$: if $g(n)=n$ this is $g(n)\le n+1$; if $g(n)=n+1$ then $2007\mid n$, so $2007\nmid n+1$ and $g(n+1)=n+1$.
- If $2007\mid m+n$: $g(m+n)=m+n+1=(m+1)+(n+1)-1\ge g(m)+g(g(n))-1$.
- If $2007\nmid m+n$, then $2007\nmid m$ or $2007\nmid n$. In the first case $g(m)=m$, so $g(m)+g(g(n))-1\le m+(n+1)-1=m+n=g(m+n)$. In the second case $g(n)=n$ and $g(g(n))=g(n)=n$, so $g(m)+g(g(n))-1\le (m+1)+n-1=g(m+n)$.

So exactly the values $1,2,\dots,2008$ are possible. ∎

imo-isl-2007-a3.title: Compare each term with $1/t$
imo-isl-2007-a3.body:
Since $x^n+y^n=1$ with $x,y>0$, both $x$ and $y$ lie in $(0,1)$.

**A one-variable estimate.** For $0<t<1$,
$$\frac1t-\frac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}=\frac{1+t^4-t-t^3}{t(1+t^4)}=\frac{(1-t)(1-t^3)}{t(1+t^4)}>0,$$
so $\dfrac{1+t^2}{1+t^4}<\dfrac1t$.

**Summing.** Apply this with $t=x^k$ ($k=1,\dots,n$):
$$0<\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+x^{2k}}{1+x^{4k}}<\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{x^k}=\frac{1}{x^n}\big(1+x+\dots+x^{n-1}\big)=\frac{1-x^n}{x^n(1-x)}=\frac{y^n}{x^n(1-x)},$$
using $1-x^n=y^n$. In the same way, using $1-y^n=x^n$,
$$0<\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+y^{2k}}{1+y^{4k}}<\frac{x^n}{y^n(1-y)}.$$

**Multiplying** the two inequalities between positive numbers:
$$\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+x^{2k}}{1+x^{4k}}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+y^{2k}}{1+y^{4k}}\right)<\frac{y^n}{x^n(1-x)}\cdot\frac{x^n}{y^n(1-y)}=\frac1{(1-x)(1-y)}.$$
∎

imo-isl-2007-a4.title: Pass to $g(x)=f(x)-x$
imo-isl-2007-a4.body:
**Step 1: $f(y)>y$ for all $y$.** The equation gives $f\big(x+f(y)\big)>f(x+y)$ for all $x$. If $f(y)=y$ this reads $f(x+y)>f(x+y)$, impossible. If $f(y)<y$, put $x=y-f(y)>0$:
$$f(y)=f\big(x+f(y)\big)=f(x+y)+f(y)>f(y),$$
again impossible. So $f(y)>y$.

**Step 2: a new equation.** Let $g(x)=f(x)-x>0$. For $t>y>0$ substitute $x=t-y$; then $x+f(y)=t+g(y)$ and the equation becomes $f\big(t+g(y)\big)=f(t)+f(y)$, i.e.
$$g\big(t+g(y)\big)+t+g(y)=g(t)+t+g(y)+y,$$
$$g\big(t+g(y)\big)=g(t)+y\qquad\text{for all } t>y>0.\qquad(2)$$

**Step 3: $g$ is injective.** If $g(y_1)=g(y_2)$, then for $t>\max\{y_1,y_2\}$, (2) gives $g(t)+y_1=g\big(t+g(y_1)\big)=g\big(t+g(y_2)\big)=g(t)+y_2$, so $y_1=y_2$.

**Step 4: $g$ is additive.** Let $u,v>0$ and $t>u+v$. Using (2) three times (note $t+g(u)>v$, $t>u$, $t>u+v$):
$$g\big(t+g(u)+g(v)\big)=g\big(t+g(u)\big)+v=g(t)+u+v=g\big(t+g(u+v)\big).$$
By injectivity, $g(u)+g(v)=g(u+v)$. As $g>0$, this also shows $g$ is strictly increasing: $g(u+v)=g(u)+g(v)>g(u)$.

**Step 5: $g(x)=x$.** From (2) and additivity, $g(t)+y=g\big(t+g(y)\big)=g(t)+g\big(g(y)\big)$, so $g\big(g(y)\big)=y$. If $g(x)<x$ for some $x$, then by monotonicity $g(g(x))<g(x)$, i.e. $x<g(x)$, a contradiction; similarly $g(x)>x$ gives $x>g(x)$. Hence $g(x)=x$ and $f(x)=2x$.

**Check.** $f\big(x+2y\big)=2x+4y=(2x+2y)+2y=f(x+y)+f(y)$. So the only solution is $f(x)=2x$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-a5.title: Weighted splitting of the binary expansion
imo-isl-2007-a5.body:
**Lemma.** Let $s_1,\dots,s_k$ be nonnegative integers with $\sum_{i=1}^k2^{-s_i}\le1$. Then for all positive integers $n_1,\dots,n_k$,
$$a\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k n_i\Big)\le\sum_{i=1}^k2^{s_i}a(n_i).$$

*Proof.* Induction on $k$. For $k=1$: $2^{s_1}\ge1$ and $a\ge0$. For $k=2$: both $s_i\ge1$ (if $s_1=0$ the sum would exceed $1$), so $a(n_1+n_2)\le2a(n_1)+2a(n_2)\le2^{s_1}a(n_1)+2^{s_2}a(n_2)$.

Let $k>2$ and order $s_1\le\dots\le s_k$. The number $\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}2^{-s_i}$ is a multiple of $2^{-s_{k-1}}$ and is less than $1$ (because $2^{-s_k}>0$), hence it is at most $1-2^{-s_{k-1}}$. Also $s_{k-1}\ge2$: otherwise $s_1=\dots=s_{k-1}=1$ and the full sum would exceed $(k-1)/2\ge1$. Put $s'=s_{k-1}-1\ge1$ and $n'=n_{k-1}+n_k$. Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}2^{-s_i}+2^{-s'}=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}2^{-s_i}+2^{-s_{k-1}}\le1,$$
so by the induction hypothesis (for $k-1$ terms)
$$a\Big(\sum_{i=1}^kn_i\Big)\le\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}2^{s_i}a(n_i)+2^{s_{k-1}-1}a(n_{k-1}+n_k)\le\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}2^{s_i}a(n_i)+2^{s_{k-1}}a(n_{k-1})+2^{s_{k-1}}a(n_k),$$
and $2^{s_{k-1}}\le2^{s_k}$. $\square$

**Main argument.** Let $q=c/2>1$. Take any positive integer $n$ and write it in binary, $n=\sum_{i=1}^k2^{u_i}$ with $0\le u_1<\dots<u_k$. Let $t_i=\lfloor q\log_2(u_i+1)\rfloor$, so that
$$2^{t_i}\le(u_i+1)^q<2^{t_i+1}.$$
Let $T=\sum_i2^{-t_i}$ and choose the integer $d$ with $2^{d-1}<T\le2^d$; set $s_i=t_i+d$. Then $\sum_i2^{-s_i}=2^{-d}T\in(\tfrac12,1]$; in particular each $2^{-s_i}\le1$, so the $s_i$ are nonnegative integers and the Lemma applies. Moreover
$$2^d<2T=2\sum_i2^{-t_i}<4\sum_i\frac1{(u_i+1)^q}.$$
Now, using $a(2^{u})\le(u+1)^{-c}=(u+1)^{-2q}$,
$$a(n)\le\sum_i2^{s_i}a\big(2^{u_i}\big)\le\sum_i2^d(u_i+1)^q\cdot\frac{1}{(u_i+1)^{2q}}=2^d\sum_i\frac1{(u_i+1)^q}<4\Big(\sum_i\frac1{(u_i+1)^q}\Big)^2.$$
The $u_i+1$ are distinct positive integers, so $\sum_i(u_i+1)^{-q}\le\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{-q}$, which is finite because $q>1$. Therefore
$$a(n)<4\Big(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac1{m^{c/2}}\Big)^2$$
for every $n$, and the sequence is bounded. ∎

imo-isl-2007-a6.title: Cauchy–Schwarz on a cleverly weighted sum
imo-isl-2007-a6.body:
Indices are taken modulo $100$ ($a_{101}=a_1$, $a_{102}=a_2$). Let $S=\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_k^2a_{k+1}$. Since $\sum_k a_{k+1}\cdot2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}=2\sum_k a_{k+1}^2a_{k+2}=2S$,
$$3S=\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_{k+1}\big(a_k^2+2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}\big).$$

**Cauchy–Schwarz** with $\sum a_{k+1}^2=1$:
$$9S^2\le\sum_{k}\big(a_k^2+2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}\big)^2=\sum_k\Big(a_k^4+4a_k^2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}+4a_{k+1}^2a_{k+2}^2\Big).$$

**AM-GM** $2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}\le a_{k+1}^2+a_{k+2}^2$ gives $4a_k^2a_{k+1}a_{k+2}\le2a_k^2a_{k+1}^2+2a_k^2a_{k+2}^2$. Since $\sum_k a_{k+1}^2a_{k+2}^2=\sum_k a_k^2a_{k+1}^2$,
$$9S^2\le\sum_k\big(a_k^4+2a_k^2a_{k+1}^2+2a_k^2a_{k+2}^2\big)+4\sum_ka_k^2a_{k+1}^2.$$

**Two simple estimates.**
- The unordered pairs $\{k,k+1\}$ and $\{k,k+2\}$ ($k=1,\dots,100$) are $200$ distinct pairs of indices, so
$$\sum_k\big(a_k^4+2a_k^2a_{k+1}^2+2a_k^2a_{k+2}^2\big)\le\sum_ka_k^4+2\sum_{i<j}a_i^2a_j^2=\Big(\sum_ka_k^2\Big)^2=1.$$
- Each pair $\{k,k+1\}$ consists of one odd and one even index (100 is even), and these pairs are distinct, so with $A=\sum_{i\text{ odd}}a_i^2$, $B=\sum_{j\text{ even}}a_j^2$,
$$\sum_ka_k^2a_{k+1}^2\le AB\le\frac{(A+B)^2}{4}=\frac14.$$

Therefore $9S^2\le1+4\cdot\frac14=2$, so
$$S\le\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\approx0.4714<0.48=\frac{12}{25}$$
(indeed $\frac29<\frac{144}{625}$). ∎

imo-isl-2007-c1.title: Block sums are forced, then induct on blocks
imo-isl-2007-c1.body:
For $0\le k\le l\le n^2+n$ write $S(k,l]=a_{k+1}+\dots+a_l$. Condition (b) says $S(i,i+n]<S(i+n,i+2n]$ for $0\le i\le n^2-n$. Split the sequence into blocks $0,1,\dots,n$ of length $n$; block $v$ consists of the positions $vn+1,\dots,vn+n$.

**Block sums.** Using (b) with $i=0,n,\dots,(n-1)n$:
$$0\le S(0,n]<S(n,2n]<\dots<S(n^2,n^2+n]\le n.$$
These are $n+1$ distinct integers in $[0,n]$, so
$$S\big(vn,(v+1)n\big]=v\qquad(0\le v\le n).\qquad(2)$$

**Claim: block $v$ is $n-v$ zeros followed by $v$ ones.** Induction on $v$. For $v=0$ the block sum is $0$.

Let $v\ge1$ and assume block $v-1$ is $n-v+1$ zeros followed by $v-1$ ones. Block $v$ has sum $v\ge1$; let its first $1$ be at its $u$-th position, i.e. $a_{vn+u}=1$ and $a_{vn+1}=\dots=a_{vn+u-1}=0$. All $v$ ones of block $v$ are at positions $\ge u$, so $u\le n-v+1$, i.e. $n-u\ge v-1$.

Consider the windows $W_t=\big(u+(t-1)n,\;u+tn\big]$ for $t=v,\dots,n$ (each has length $n$; the last ends at $u+n^2\le n^2+n$). Window $W_v$ consists of the last $n-u$ positions of block $v-1$ — which contain all its $v-1$ ones, as $n-u\ge v-1$ — and the first $u$ positions of block $v$, containing exactly one $1$. So $S(W_v)=v$. Condition (b) with $i=u+(t-1)n$ (allowed for $t\le n-1$, since $u\ge1$) gives
$$v=S(W_v)<S(W_{v+1})<\dots<S(W_n)\le n,$$
$n-v+1$ distinct integers in $[v,n]$; hence $S(W_t)=t$ for all $t$.

Now compute the sum of the positions from $u+(v-1)n+1$ to $n^2+n$ in two ways.
- By windows: $\sum_{t=v}^nS(W_t)$ plus the last $n-u$ positions of block $n$, which are all ones by (2): total $\sum_{t=v}^nt+(n-u)$.
- By blocks: the last $n-u$ positions of block $v-1$ (sum $v-1$) plus blocks $v,\dots,n$: total $(v-1)+\sum_{t=v}^nt$.

Hence $n-u=v-1$, i.e. $u=n-v+1$. So the first $n-v$ positions of block $v$ are zeros, and the remaining $v$ positions carry the sum $v$, so they are all ones. This proves the claim, and therefore the sequence is the one described (position $u+vn$ holds $1$ exactly when $u\ge n-v+1$).

**This sequence works.** Write $i=u+vn$ with $1\le u\le n$, $0\le v\le n-1$. Then $a_i=[u+v\ge n+1]$ and $a_{i+n}=[u+v\ge n]$, so $a_i\le a_{i+n}$, with strict inequality exactly when $u+v=n$, i.e. at the *jump positions* $i=n+v(n-1)$, $v=0,\dots,n-1$; these run from $n$ to $n^2-n+1$ with gaps $n-1$. For $0\le i\le n^2-n$,
$$S(i+n,i+2n]-S(i,i+n]=\sum_{j=i+1}^{i+n}(a_{j+n}-a_j)$$
is a sum of nonnegative terms, and it is positive as soon as $[i+1,i+n]$ contains a jump position. It does: let $J$ be the largest jump position $\le i+n$ (exists since $i+n\ge n$). If $J\le i$, then $J<n^2-n+1$ is not the last jump, and the next one, $J+n-1\le i+n-1$, contradicts the choice of $J$. So (b) holds, and the sequence above is the unique solution. ∎

imo-isl-2007-c2.title: Minimal counterexample
imo-isl-2007-c2.body:
Call a horizontal or vertical line that meets the interior of the square but not the interior of any rectangle a *splitting line*, and a rectangle with no point on the boundary of the square an *interior rectangle*. Suppose there is a dissection into more than one rectangle with no splitting line and no interior rectangle, and take one with the smallest number $N$ of rectangles. Then $N>2$: two rectangles tiling the square are separated by a full segment parallel to a side, which lies on a splitting line.

**No two rectangles share a whole side.** Otherwise replace them by their union, which is a rectangle. The new dissection has $N-1\ge2$ rectangles; a line meeting the interior of one of the two old rectangles meets the interior of the union, so there is still no splitting line, and the union touches the boundary because each old rectangle did. This contradicts the minimality of $N$.

Let the square be $ABCD$ with $A$ lower left, $B$ lower right, $C$ upper right, $D$ upper left, and use coordinates with $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$. Let $a$ and $b$ be the rectangles containing $A$ and $B$. Then $a\ne b$: otherwise this rectangle spans the full width and its top side lies on a splitting line. Let $a=[0,w]\times[0,h_a]$ ($w<1$) and let $h_b$ be the height of $b$; by symmetry we may assume $h_a\le h_b$. Let $c$ be the rectangle whose lower left corner is $(w,0)$, with height $h_c$. If $h_c=h_a$, then $a$ and $c$ would share the whole side $\{w\}\times[0,h_a]$; so $h_c\ne h_a$.

**Case 1: $h_c<h_a$.** Let $d$ be the rectangle containing the points just above the top left corner $(w,h_c)$ of $c$. Points just to the left of $x=w$ at those heights lie in $a$ and points just below $y=h_c$ lie in $c$, so $d$ has its left side on $x=w$ and its bottom on $y=h_c$. Thus $d$ does not touch $AB$ or $AD$. It does not touch $BC$ either: otherwise $d$ would contain points $(1-\varepsilon,h_c+\varepsilon)$, which lie in $b$ because $h_c<h_a\le h_b$. So $d$ touches $CD$, and its left side is $\{w\}\times[h_c,1]$. Now the vertical line $x=w$ is bordered by $a$ on $0<y<h_a$ and by $d$ on $h_c<y<1$; since $h_c<h_a$ these cover $(0,1)$, so no rectangle's interior crosses $x=w$: a splitting line. Contradiction.

**Case 2: $h_c>h_a$.** Let $d$ be the rectangle containing the points just above the top right corner $(w,h_a)$ of $a$, on the left of $x=w$. Points just to the right of $x=w$ there lie in $c$, and points just below lie in $a$, so $d$ has its right side on $x=w$ and its bottom on $y=h_a$. Then $d$ does not touch $AB$ or $BC$. It does not touch $AD$ either: then its bottom side would be $[0,w]\times\{h_a\}$, the whole top side of $a$, which is forbidden. So $d$ touches $CD$, and its right side is $\{w\}\times[h_a,1]$. The line $x=w$ is bordered by $a$ on $(0,h_a)$ and by $d$ on $(h_a,1)$, so it is a splitting line. Contradiction.

Hence every dissection without splitting lines contains an interior rectangle. ∎

imo-isl-2007-c3.title: Count the monochromatic triples
imo-isl-2007-c3.body:
Let $R$ and $B$ be the red and blue numbers, $|R|=r$, $|B|=b$, $r+b=n$. Call a triple *divisible* if $n\mid x+y+z$.

**Claim: there are exactly $r^2-rb+b^2$ monochromatic divisible triples.** For each pair $(x,y)\in S\times S$ there is exactly one $z\in S$ with $n\mid x+y+z$, so there are $n^2$ divisible triples. In a bichromatic divisible triple $(x,y,z)$ two entries have one colour and one has the other, so exactly one of the cyclically consecutive pairs $(x,y),(y,z),(z,x)$ lies in $R\times B$; assign this pair to the triple. Conversely, for $(x,y)\in R\times B$ with $z$ the completing element, the triples $(x,y,z),(y,z,x),(z,x,y)$ are distinct (as $x\ne y$), all divisible and bichromatic, and $(x,y)$ is assigned to each of them, and to no other triple. So the number of bichromatic divisible triples is $3rb$, and the number of monochromatic ones is
$$n^2-3rb=(r+b)^2-3rb=r^2-rb+b^2.$$
(It depends only on $r$ and $b$, so any colouring with these sizes works.)

**Solving $r^2-rb+b^2=2007=9\cdot223$.** Since $9\mid(r+b)^2-3rb$, we get $3\mid(r+b)^2$, so $3\mid r+b$, then $9\mid(r+b)^2$ gives $9\mid3rb$, so $3\mid rb$; together with $3\mid r+b$ this forces $3\mid r$ and $3\mid b$. Write $r=3s$, $b=3t$ with $s\ge t\ge0$ (by symmetry): $s^2-st+t^2=223$.

Bounds for $s$: $4\cdot223=892=(2t-s)^2+3s^2\ge3s^2$, so $s^2\le297$; and $223=s^2-t(s-t)\le s^2$. Thus $15\le s\le17$, and $t(s-t)=s^2-223$:
- $s=15$: $t(15-t)=2$, no integer solution;
- $s=16$: $t(16-t)=33$, no integer solution (discriminant $256-132=124$ is not a square);
- $s=17$: $t(17-t)=66$, so $t=6$ or $t=11$.

So $(r,b)=(51,18)$ or $(51,33)$ (up to swapping colours), giving $n=69$ or $n=84$. Both work: $51^2-51\cdot18+18^2=2007$ and $51^2-51\cdot33+33^2=2007$.

**Answer: $n=69$ and $n=84$.** ∎

imo-isl-2007-c4.title: Sum of squares increases
imo-isl-2007-c4.body:
**Lemma.** If $|x_i|<a$ for all $i$, there is a partition $\{1,\dots,n\}=I\cup J$ with $\big|\sum_{I}x_i-\sum_Jx_j\big|<a$.

*Proof.* Induction on $n$; for $n=1$ take $I=\{1\}$. For $n>1$, take a partition $I'\cup J'$ of $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ with $D=\sum_{I'}x_i-\sum_{J'}x_j\in(-a,a)$; swapping $I'$ and $J'$ if necessary, $D\in[0,a)$. If $x_n\ge0$ put $n$ into $J$, otherwise into $I$. In both cases the new difference is $D-|x_n|$ with $D,|x_n|\in[0,a)$, hence lies in $(-a,a)$. $\square$

**The problem.** Suppose, to the contrary, that all entries of all $A_k$ lie in $(-n/2,n/2)$.

*Finitely many states.* The $i$-th entry of every $A_k$ differs from $a_i$ by an integer, and an open interval of length $n$ contains at most $n$ numbers of the form $a_i+(\text{integer})$. So at most $n^n$ different sequences can occur, and $A_p=A_q$ for some $p<q$.

*Sum of squares.* Let $S_k$ be the sum of squares of the entries of $A_k$. If $A_k=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $I\cup J$ is the partition used, then by the Lemma (with $a=n/2$) the minimal value satisfies $\big|\sum_Ix_i-\sum_Jx_j\big|<n/2$, so
$$S_{k+1}-S_k=\sum_{i\in I}\big((x_i+1)^2-x_i^2\big)+\sum_{j\in J}\big((x_j-1)^2-x_j^2\big)=n+2\Big(\sum_{I}x_i-\sum_Jx_j\Big)>n-2\cdot\frac n2=0.$$
Thus $S_p<S_{p+1}<\dots<S_q$, contradicting $A_p=A_q$. Hence some $A_k$ contains an element $x$ with $|x|\ge n/2$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-c5.title: Force a periodic colouring, then tilt the rectangle
imo-isl-2007-c5.body:
The colour of a point is the colour of the strip containing it, so it depends only on its $x$-coordinate.

**Axis-parallel rectangles.** If $S_n$ and $S_{n+a}$ have the same colour, the rectangle with vertices $(n,0),(n,b),(n+a,0),(n+a,b)$ works; similarly if $S_n$ and $S_{n+b}$ have the same colour. So assume that $S_n$ and $S_{n+a}$, as well as $S_n$ and $S_{n+b}$, have opposite colours for every $n$. By induction on $|p|+|q|$, $S_n$ and $S_{n+pa+qb}$ have the same colour if and only if $p+q$ is even.

**Consequences.** Let $d=\gcd(a,b)$, $a=a_1d$, $b=b_1d$. Since $b_1a-a_1b=0$, taking $p=b_1$, $q=-a_1$ shows $b_1-a_1$ is even; as $a_1,b_1$ are coprime, both are odd. We may assume $a>b$, so $a_1>b_1\ge1$ and $a_1\ge3$. Choose integers $k,\ell$ with $ka_1-\ell b_1=1$, i.e. $ka-\ell b=d$. Reducing mod $2$ (with $a_1,b_1$ odd), $k-\ell\equiv1$, so $k-\ell$ is odd: **$S_n$ and $S_{n+d}$ always have opposite colours**, and hence the colouring has period $2d$.

**A tilted rectangle.** Let $\varphi=\sqrt{a_1^2-4}$. It is irrational: $(a_1-1)^2<a_1^2-4<a_1^2$ for $a_1\ge3$. Put the rectangle $ABCD$ (with $AB=CD=a$, $AD=BC=b$) so that the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $(2d,\,d\varphi)$ — its length is $d\sqrt{4+a_1^2-4}=a$ — and $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac{b}{a}(d\varphi,\,-2d)$, which is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and has length $b$. If $A$ has $x$-coordinate $t$, then the $x$-coordinates are
$$A:\ t,\qquad B:\ t+2d,\qquad D:\ u,\qquad C:\ u+2d,\qquad\text{where } u=t+\theta,\ \theta=\frac{bd\varphi}{a}=\frac{b_1d}{a_1}\varphi.$$
By the period $2d$, $A,B$ have the same colour and $C,D$ have the same colour. So it suffices to choose $t$ with $t$ and $t+\theta$ of the same colour. Note that $\theta$ is irrational.

**Choosing $t$.** Let $w$ be the maximal number of consecutive strips of the same colour ($w\le d$, because $S_n$ and $S_{n+d}$ differ), and let $S_{n_0},\dots,S_{n_0+w-1}$ be such a run, say red. The interval $I=(n_0+\theta,\;n_0+\theta+w)$ has length $w$ and non-integer endpoints, so it meets $w+1$ consecutive strips; these cannot all be blue (a run longer than $w$), so $I$ contains a point $u$ of a red strip. Then $t=u-\theta\in(n_0,n_0+w)$ lies in a red strip too. With this $t$, all four vertices $A,B,C,D$ are red. ∎

imo-isl-2007-c7.title: Block construction
imo-isl-2007-c7.body:
Let $k,m$ be positive integers (chosen later), $n=km$, and split $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into disjoint blocks $A_1,\dots,A_k$ of size $m$. Define
$$\mathcal S=\{S:\ S\cap A_i\ne\varnothing\text{ for all } i\},\qquad\mathcal T_1=\{T:\ A_i\subseteq T\text{ for some } i\},\qquad\mathcal T=\mathcal T_1\setminus\mathcal S.$$
If $S\in\mathcal S$ and $T\in\mathcal T$, take $i$ with $A_i\subseteq T$; then $S\cap T\supseteq S\cap A_i\ne\varnothing$. The families $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal T$ are disjoint, so if $|\mathcal S|,|\mathcal T|>\alpha2^n$ we can take $p=\min(|\mathcal S|,|\mathcal T|)$ and pick $S_1,\dots,S_p\in\mathcal S$ and $T_1,\dots,T_p\in\mathcal T$, all distinct.

**Counting.** A set is determined by its intersections with the blocks.
- $S\in\mathcal S$: each $S\cap A_i$ is one of the $2^m-1$ nonempty subsets, so $|\mathcal S|=(2^m-1)^k$.
- A set not in $\mathcal T_1$ has each $H\cap A_i\ne A_i$: $(2^m-1)^k$ sets, so $|\mathcal T_1|=2^{km}-(2^m-1)^k$.
- $\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal T_1$: each intersection is neither $\varnothing$ nor $A_i$, so $|\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal T_1|=(2^m-2)^k$.

Hence
$$|\mathcal T|=|\mathcal T_1|-|\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T_1|=|\mathcal T_1|-\big(|\mathcal S|-|\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal T_1|\big)=2^{km}-2(2^m-1)^k+(2^m-2)^k.$$

**Choosing $k$.** Let $\delta=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}$, a root of $\delta^2-3\delta+1=0$, so $1-2\delta+\delta^2=\delta$. Put $k=\big\lfloor2^m\ln\frac1\delta\big\rfloor$. Since $k\ln(1-2^{-m})=-k2^{-m}+O(k4^{-m})\to-\ln\frac1\delta$ and likewise $k\ln(1-2\cdot2^{-m})\to-2\ln\frac1\delta$ as $m\to\infty$,
$$\frac{|\mathcal S|}{2^{km}}=\Big(1-\frac1{2^m}\Big)^k\to\delta,\qquad\frac{|\mathcal T|}{2^{km}}=1-2\Big(1-\frac1{2^m}\Big)^k+\Big(1-\frac2{2^m}\Big)^k\to1-2\delta+\delta^2=\delta.$$
Since $\alpha<\delta$, for $m$ large enough both ratios exceed $\alpha$, i.e. $|\mathcal S|,|\mathcal T|>\alpha\cdot2^n$, and we are done. ∎

imo-isl-2007-c8.title: Assign triangles to extreme neighbours
imo-isl-2007-c8.body:
**Assignments.** For a vertex $A$, the other vertices of the good triangles through $A$ lie on the unit circle $\omega_A$ centred at $A$. Since $P$ is convex, all other vertices of $P$ lie inside the angle of $P$ at $A$, which is less than $180^\circ$; so these partner points lie on an arc of $\omega_A$ of less than $180^\circ$. Let $L_A$ be the extreme one in the counterclockwise direction and $R_A$ the extreme one in the clockwise direction. The segment $AL_A$ is a side of exactly one good triangle: the third vertex is $L_A$ rotated about $A$ by $\pm60^\circ$, and the rotation beyond $L_A$ is impossible by extremality. Assign this triangle to $A$ *counterclockwise*; similarly assign the good triangle on $AR_A$ to $A$ *clockwise* (if $A$ lies in only one good triangle, it receives both assignments). There are at most $2n$ assignments in total.

**Each good triangle gets at least three assignments.** Let $ABC$ be good with vertices in clockwise order. We show: *$ABC$ is assigned counterclockwise to $C$ or clockwise to $B$.* By cyclic symmetry it is then also assigned counterclockwise to $A$ or clockwise to $C$, and counterclockwise to $B$ or clockwise to $A$ — three different (vertex, direction) slots. Hence $3t\le2n$, where $t$ is the number of good triangles.

Place $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=\big(\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\big)$ (a clockwise unit triangle; a rotation and translation achieve this). Measure directions as angles counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Seen from $C$: $A$ is at $120^\circ$, $B$ at $60^\circ$. Seen from $B$: $A$ is at $180^\circ$, $C$ at $240^\circ$. So $ABC$ is assigned counterclockwise to $C$ iff $L_C=A$, and clockwise to $B$ iff $R_B=A$. Suppose $L_C\ne A$ and $R_B\ne A$.

*A point $X$ near $A$ on $\omega_C$.* The direction $\lambda$ of $L_C$ from $C$ is $>120^\circ$, and $<240^\circ$ because $B$ (at $60^\circ$) lies within the same arc of less than $180^\circ$. The good triangle on $CL_C$ has third vertex $L_C'$ at direction $\lambda-60^\circ$. Let $X=L_C$ if $\lambda\le180^\circ$ and $X=L_C'$ otherwise; then $X$ is a vertex of $P$ on $\omega_C$ at direction $\theta\in(120^\circ,180^\circ]$ from $C$.

*A point $Y$ near $A$ on $\omega_B$.* Similarly the direction $\rho$ of $R_B$ from $B$ lies in $(60^\circ,180^\circ)$, the third vertex on $BR_B$ is at $\rho+60^\circ$, and we get a vertex $Y$ of $P$ on $\omega_B$ at direction $\phi\in[120^\circ,180^\circ)$ from $B$.

*Directions from $A$.* For two points $O+e^{i\alpha}$, $O+e^{i\beta}$ on a unit circle, $e^{i\beta}-e^{i\alpha}=2i\sin\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}\,e^{i(\alpha+\beta)/2}$. With $O=C$, $\alpha=120^\circ$, $\beta=\theta$, the direction of $\overrightarrow{AX}$ is $\frac{\theta+120^\circ}{2}+90^\circ\in(210^\circ,240^\circ]$. With $O=B$, $\alpha=180^\circ$, $\beta=\phi$, the direction of $\overrightarrow{AY}$ is $\frac{\phi+180^\circ}{2}-90^\circ\in[60^\circ,90^\circ)$. Also $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is at $0^\circ$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ at $300^\circ$. In circular order $B,Y,X,C$, the consecutive angular gaps are at most $90^\circ$, at most $180^\circ$, at most $90^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ — none exceeds $180^\circ$. Hence the four vectors do not all lie in an open half-plane, so $A$ lies in the convex hull of $X,Y,B,C$ (possibly on the segment $XY$).

But $X,Y,B,C$ are vertices of $P$ different from $A$ ($X\ne Y$ since $\omega_B\cap\omega_C=\{A,\,B+C-A\}$), and a vertex of a convex polygon cannot lie in the convex hull of other vertices. This contradiction proves the claim, and so $t\le\frac23n$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-g2.title: Midpoint of $BT$ and the circle on $XT$
imo-isl-2007-g2.body:
Let $N$ be the midpoint of $BT$.

- Since $XB=XT$, the line $XN$ is the axis of symmetry of the isosceles triangle $BXT$: $\angle XNT=90^\circ$ and $\angle BXN=\angle NXT$.
- In triangle $BCT$, $M$ and $N$ are midpoints of $BC$ and $BT$, so $MN\parallel CT$ and $\angle CTM=\angle NMT$ (alternate angles).
- Because $\angle XMT=\angle XNT=90^\circ$, the points $M$ and $N$ lie on the circle with diameter $XT$.

Inscribed angles in this circle give
$$\angle MTB=\angle MTN=\angle MXN,\qquad \angle CTM=\angle NMT=\angle NXT=\angle BXN.$$
Therefore
$$\angle MTB-\angle CTM=\angle MXN-\angle BXN=\angle MXB=\angle MAB,$$
the last equality being an inscribed angle in the circle $ABM$ (on which $X$ lies). This angle depends only on the triangle, not on $X$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-g2.title: Reflect $T$ in $M$
imo-isl-2007-g2.body:
Let $S$ be the reflection of $T$ in $M$. Since $XM\perp TS$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $TS$, $XM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $TS$, so $XS=XT=XB$: $X$ is the circumcentre of triangle $BST$, and $XM$ bisects $\angle SXT$.

The point reflection in $M$ swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$ and $T\leftrightarrow S$, so $\angle BSM=\angle CTM$. Using inscribed versus central angles in the circle centred at $X$:
$$\angle MTB-\angle CTM=\angle STB-\angle BST=\frac{\angle SXB}{2}-\frac{\angle BXT}{2}.$$
Moreover $\angle SXB=\angle SXT-\angle BXT=2\angle MXT-\angle BXT$. Hence
$$\angle MTB-\angle CTM=\frac{2\angle MXT-2\angle BXT}{2}=\angle MXT-\angle BXT=\angle MXB=\angle MAB,$$
which is constant. ∎

imo-isl-2007-g3.title: A homothety centred at $P$
imo-isl-2007-g3.body:
Let $t=\frac{AD}{BC}$. Triangles $PDA$ and $PBC$ are similar with ratio $t$ and $P$ lies between $B$ and $D$ and between $A$ and $C$; so the homothety $h$ with centre $P$ and ratio $-t$ maps $B\mapsto D$ and $C\mapsto A$, and the line $BC$ onto the line $AD$. Let $Q'=h(Q)$; then $Q,P,Q'$ are collinear with $P$ between $Q$ and $Q'$.

**$Q'$ lies on the same side of $AD$ as $Q$.** The points $Q$ and $P$ lie on the same side of $BC$ (both are between the parallel lines), so $h(Q)=Q'$ and $h(P)=P$ lie on the same side of $h(BC)=AD$; and $P$ and $Q$ are on the same side of $AD$. Also, $Q$ is on the same side of $BD$ as $C$ (it lies beyond $CD$, away from $P$), so $Q'=h(Q)$ is on the same side of $BD$ as $h(C)=A$.

**A cyclic quadrilateral.** A homothety preserves angles, so
$$\angle AQ'D=\angle h(C)\,h(Q)\,h(B)=\angle CQB=\angle AQD.$$
As $Q$ and $Q'$ lie on the same side of $AD$, the points $A,Q',Q,D$ are concyclic; by the side information above they lie on the circle in this order, so $A$ and $Q'$ are on the same arc cut off by the chord $DQ$.

**Conclusion.** Using inscribed angles on chord $DQ$, then that $P$ lies on segment $Q'Q$, then the homothety once more ($h$ maps $Q\mapsto Q'$, $B\mapsto D$, $P\mapsto P$):
$$\angle DAQ=\angle DQ'Q=\angle DQ'P=\angle BQP.$$
∎

imo-isl-2007-g5.title: Pascal's theorem and the midlines
imo-isl-2007-g5.body:
Let $A_0=BB'\cap CC'$, $B_0=CC'\cap AA'$, $C_0=AA'\cap BB'$. We show $[A_0B_0C_0]=\frac12[ABC]$.

**The vertices lie on the midlines.** Apply Pascal's theorem to the inscribed hexagon $ABCC'PA'$. Its pairs of opposite sides meet at
$$AB\cap C'P=C_1,\qquad BC\cap PA'=A_1,\qquad CC'\cap A'A=B_0,$$
so these three points are collinear: $B_0$ lies on the midline $A_1C_1$. In the same way $A_0$ lies on $B_1C_1$ and $C_0$ lies on $A_1B_1$.

**A product of lengths.** The points $A,B_0,C_0$ lie on line $AA'$, and $A_1,B_1,C_0$ lie on line $A_1B_1$. Since $A_1C_1\parallel AC$ (i.e. $B_0A_1\parallel AB_1$), triangles $C_0B_0A_1$ and $C_0AB_1$ are similar:
$$\frac{B_0C_0}{AC_0}=\frac{A_1C_0}{B_1C_0}.$$
Similarly $B,A_0,C_0$ lie on $BB'$, and $B_1C_1\parallel BC$ gives similar triangles $C_0A_1B$ and $C_0B_1A_0$:
$$\frac{A_1C_0}{B_1C_0}=\frac{BC_0}{A_0C_0}.$$
Combining, $A_0C_0\cdot B_0C_0=AC_0\cdot BC_0$.

**The area.** The lines $C_0A_0$ and $C_0B_0$ are the lines $C_0B$ and $C_0A$, so the angles $\angle A_0C_0B_0$ and $\angle AC_0B$ are equal or supplementary and have the same sine. Hence
$$[A_0B_0C_0]=\tfrac12A_0C_0\cdot B_0C_0\sin\angle A_0C_0B_0=\tfrac12AC_0\cdot BC_0\sin\angle AC_0B=[ABC_0].$$
Finally $C_0$ lies on the midline $A_1B_1\parallel AB$, whose distance from $AB$ is half the altitude from $C$, so $[ABC_0]=\frac12[ABC]$. Thus the area of the triangle formed by $AA',BB',CC'$ is always $\frac12[ABC]$, independent of $P$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-g6.title: Example for $k\ge1$, then a lemma on inscribed triangles
imo-isl-2007-g6.body:
Write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area and call $AA_1D_1$, $BB_1A_1$, $CC_1B_1$, $DD_1C_1$ the *border triangles*.

**$k\ge1$.** Take a triangle $ABC$ of area $1$ with midpoints $A_1$ of $AB$, $B_1$ of $BC$, $K$ of $AC$. Choose $D$ on the extension of $BK$ beyond $K$, close to $K$ (so $ABCD$ is convex), and $C_1,D_1$ on $CD,DA$ close to $D$. As $D,C_1,D_1\to K$: $[BB_1A_1]=\frac14$, $[AA_1D_1]\to[AA_1K]=\frac14$, $[CC_1B_1]\to[CKB_1]=\frac14$, $[DD_1C_1]\to0$, and $[A_1B_1C_1D_1]\to[A_1B_1K]=\frac14$. So $S\to\frac14$ and $S_1\to\frac14$; their ratio tends to $1$, so no $k<1$ works.

**Lemma.** If $A_1,B_1,C_1$ lie on the sides $BC,CA,AB$ of a triangle $ABC$, then
$$[A_1B_1C_1]\ge\min\{[AC_1B_1],[BA_1C_1],[CB_1A_1]\}.$$
*Proof.* Let $A',B',C'$ be the midpoints of $BC,CA,AB$.

*Case (i): two of the points lie in one corner triangle*, say $B_1,C_1$ in $AC'B'$. Let $X=B_1C_1\cap AA_1$; then $X$ lies in triangle $AC'B'$, i.e. in the half of segment $AA_1$ next to $A$, so $A_1X\ge AX$. The triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $AB_1C_1$ share the base $B_1C_1$, so $\frac{[A_1B_1C_1]}{[AC_1B_1]}=\frac{A_1X}{AX}\ge1$.

*Case (ii): otherwise* each corner triangle contains exactly one of the points (each point lies in one of its two adjacent corner triangles, and a midpoint would lie in two). Up to reflection, $BA_1<BA'$, $CB_1<CB'$, $AC_1<AC'$. By Menelaus, line $A_1B_1$ meets line $AB$ at a point $Y$ beyond $B$; as $C_1$ lies on segment $AC'$, $YC_1>YC'$, so $[A_1B_1C_1]>[A_1B_1C']$ (common base $A_1B_1$). Likewise line $A_1C'$ meets line $CA$ at $Z$ beyond $A$, and $B_1$ lies on segment $B'C$, so $ZB_1>ZB'$ and $[A_1B_1C']>[A_1B'C']$ (common base $A_1C'$). Since $A_1A'\parallel B'C'$, $[A_1B'C']=[A'B'C']=\frac14[ABC]$. So $[A_1B_1C_1]>\frac14[ABC]$, and as the four triangles partition $ABC$, one of the three corner triangles has area $<\frac14[ABC]<[A_1B_1C_1]$. $\square$

**$k=1$ works.** Call triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ *small* if $[A_1B_1C_1]$ is less than both $[BB_1A_1]$ and $[CC_1B_1]$ (the border triangles at the two vertices $B$, $C$ it "spans"), and *big* otherwise; define this similarly for $B_1C_1D_1$ (compare with the border triangles at $C,D$), $C_1D_1A_1$ (at $D,A$) and $D_1A_1B_1$ (at $A,B$). If $A_1B_1C_1$ and $C_1D_1A_1$ are both big, then each is at least as large as some border triangle, and these two border triangles are different, so
$$S_1=[A_1B_1C_1]+[C_1D_1A_1]\ge S.$$
The same holds if $B_1C_1D_1$ and $D_1A_1B_1$ are both big. So suppose each of the two pairs contains a small triangle. The two small triangles share a side, so after a cyclic relabelling we may assume that $A_1B_1C_1$ and $D_1A_1B_1$ are small, and after the reflection swapping $A\leftrightarrow C$ (which swaps these two triangles) that $[A_1B_1C_1]\le[D_1A_1B_1]$. Thus
$$[A_1B_1C_1]<[BB_1A_1],\quad [A_1B_1C_1]<[CC_1B_1],\quad [A_1B_1C_1]\le[D_1A_1B_1]<[AA_1D_1].$$
We now find a triangle with vertex $B$, sides along rays $BA$ and $BC$, and third side through $C_1$, in which $A_1B_1C_1$ is inscribed and all three corner triangles are larger than $A_1B_1C_1$. That contradicts the Lemma.

*Case 1: lines $CD$ and $AB$ meet at a point $K$ beyond $A$* (then $D$ lies between $C$ and $K$). Use triangle $KBC$: $A_1\in BK$, $B_1\in BC$, $C_1\in CK$. Its corners are $BB_1A_1$, $CC_1B_1$ and $KA_1C_1$. The segment $AD$ lies in triangle $KA_1C_1$ ($A$ on side $KA_1$, $D$ on side $KC_1$), so $[KA_1C_1]\ge[AA_1D_1]>[A_1B_1C_1]$. All three corners exceed $[A_1B_1C_1]$.

*Case 2: otherwise.* Note $C_1\ne C$ (else $[CC_1B_1]=0$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ could not be small). Use oblique coordinates with origin $B$, $x$-axis along ray $BA$ and $y$-axis along ray $BC$, with $C=(0,c)$ and $C_1=(x_0,y_0)$, where $x_0,y_0>0$ because $C_1$ lies inside angle $ABC$. If $y_0<c$, the line $CD=CC_1$ would meet the $x$-axis at $k=\frac{cx_0}{c-y_0}>0$, i.e. on ray $BA$; it cannot meet segment $AB$ (the side $CD$ of a convex quadrilateral leaves $A,B$ on one side), so this would be Case 1. Hence $y_0\ge c$. For any $K=(k,0)$ with $k>x_0$, the line $KC_1$ meets the $y$-axis at $L=\big(0,\frac{ky_0}{k-x_0}\big)$ with $\frac{ky_0}{k-x_0}>y_0\ge c$, i.e. beyond $C$. Choose $k$ so large that $[KA_1C_1]=\frac12KA_1\cdot d(C_1,AB)$ exceeds $[A_1B_1C_1]$. In triangle $KBL$ the corners are $BB_1A_1$, $KA_1C_1$ and $LC_1B_1$, and $[LC_1B_1]>[CC_1B_1]>[A_1B_1C_1]$ because $B_1L>B_1C$. Again all three corners exceed $[A_1B_1C_1]$.

In both cases the Lemma is contradicted. Hence $S_1\ge S$ always, and the smallest $k$ is $1$.

**Answer: $k=1$.** ∎

imo-isl-2007-g7.title: Prove $\angle KID=\frac{\beta-\gamma}2$ first
imo-isl-2007-g7.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcentre, $P$ the point of the circumcircle opposite to $A$, and $M$ the second intersection of $AI$ with the circumcircle (the midpoint of arc $BC$, so $MB=MC=MI$). Let $A_1,B_1,T$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ to $BC$, $CA$, $AD$; let $r$ be the inradius.

**Step 1: $AM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $KP$.** It is well known that $\angle BAD=\angle CAO=90^\circ-\beta$, so $AI$ bisects $\angle DAO$, i.e. $\angle KAM=\angle MAP$. As $AK=AP=2R$, triangle $AKP$ is isosceles with apex bisector $AM$, so $AM\perp KP$; since $\angle AMP=90^\circ$ ($AP$ is a diameter), $M$ is the midpoint of $KP$. In particular $MK=MP$ and $\angle KMI=90^\circ$.

**Step 2: $\angle KID=\angle IAD$.** $DA_1IT$ is a rectangle, so $TD=IA_1=r=IB_1$. The quadrilateral $AB_1IT$ is cyclic (right angles at $T$, $B_1$), hence
$$\angle B_1TI=\angle B_1AI=\tfrac\alpha2=\angle BAM=\angle BPM,\qquad \angle IB_1T=\angle IAT=\angle MAK=\angle MAP=\angle MBP.$$
So triangles $B_1TI$ and $BPM$ are similar, and $\frac{IT}{IB_1}=\frac{MP}{MB}$. Therefore
$$\frac{IT}{TD}=\frac{IT}{IB_1}=\frac{MP}{MB}=\frac{KM}{MI},$$
so the right triangles $ITD$ (right angle at $T$) and $KMI$ (right angle at $M$) are similar, with $I\leftrightarrow K$, $D\leftrightarrow I$. Hence $\angle KIM=\angle IDT=\angle IDA$, and, since $\angle MID$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AID$,
$$\angle KID=\angle MID-\angle KIM=(\angle IAD+\angle IDA)-\angle IDA=\angle IAD.$$
Finally $\angle IAD=\angle IAB-\angle DAB=\frac\alpha2-(90^\circ-\beta)=\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2}$. So
$$\angle KID=\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2}.\qquad(1)$$

**Step 3: where $F$ is.** Since $\beta>\gamma$, the order on $BC$ is $B,D,A_1,C$. As $AD>2r$, we have $DT=r<AD-r=AT$, hence $DI<AI$ and $\angle IAD<\angle IDA$. Also $\angle DIA_1=\angle IDA$ (because $IA_1\parallel AD$). So $\angle KID=\angle IAD<\angle DIA_1$, and $K$, $A_1$ lie on the same side of line $DI$; hence ray $IK$ lies inside angle $DIA_1$, and $F$ lies strictly between $D$ and $A_1$. Note $F$ lies between $K$ and $I$, while $I$ lies between $D$ and $E$, so $\angle EIF=180^\circ-\angle KID$. Also $\angle IFC=\angle IFA_1<90^\circ$.

**Step 4: use $IE=IF$.** Since $IB_1=IA_1=r$, the right triangles $IEB_1$ and $IFA_1$ are congruent, so $\angle IEB_1=\angle IFA_1=\angle IFC$ (acute). ($E\ne B_1$, otherwise $F=A_1$.)

- *$E$ between $C$ and $B_1$.* Then $\angle IEA=\angle IEB_1=\angle IFC$, so $\angle IEC+\angle IFC=180^\circ$ and $CEIF$ is cyclic. Hence $\gamma=\angle ECF=180^\circ-\angle EIF=\angle KID=\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2}$, i.e. $\beta=3\gamma$.
- *$E$ between $A$ and $B_1$.* Then $\angle IEC=\angle IEB_1=\angle IFC<90^\circ$, and in the convex quadrilateral $CEIF$,
$$\gamma=360^\circ-\angle EIF-2\angle IFC>180^\circ-\angle EIF=\angle KID=\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2},$$
so $\beta<3\gamma$.

In both cases $\beta\le3\gamma$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-g8.title: Homothety centres of $\omega$ and $\Omega$
imo-isl-2007-g8.body:
We use the **three homothety centres theorem**: if $h_1$ is a homothety with centre $O_1$ and $h_2$ one with centre $O_2\ne O_1$, and $h_2\circ h_1$ is a homothety, then its centre lies on line $O_1O_2$; its ratio is the product of the two ratios. Also recall that for two circles with different centres there is exactly one homothety with positive ratio and exactly one with negative ratio taking one to the other (when the radii differ, for the positive one), and both centres lie on the line of centres.

Let $\Omega$ be the circle tangent to segment $AB$ and to rays $AD$ and $BC$ (its centre $J$ is the intersection of the bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle ABC$). Let $\omega_A,\omega_B$ be the incircles of $APD$ and $BPC$. We show $E$ and $F$ lie on $IJ$ (if $I=J$, then $E=F=I$ by the same arguments and there is nothing to prove).

**$F$ lies on $IJ$.** $\omega$ and $\omega_A$ lie on opposite sides of $PD$ and touch at $K$, so the homothety $\omega\to\omega_A$ with centre $K$ has negative ratio. $\omega_A$ and $\Omega$ are both inscribed in the angle $DAB$, so $\omega_A\to\Omega$ is a homothety with centre $A$ and positive ratio. The composition takes $\omega$ to $\Omega$ with negative ratio, so its centre — the unique negative homothety centre of $\omega$ and $\Omega$ — lies on line $AK$. In the same way (via $L$ and $B$) it lies on line $BL$. Hence it is $F$, and $F$ lies on the line of centres $IJ$.

**$APCD$ and $BCDP$ have incircles.** Both $\omega$ and $\omega_A$ are tangent to line $PD$ and touch each other at $K$, from opposite sides, so they touch $PD$ at the same point $K$. Let $\omega$ touch $PC$, $CD$ at $X$, $Y$, and let $\omega_A$ touch $AP$, $AD$ at $U$, $V$. Equal tangents give
$$AP+CD=(AU+PK)+(CX+DK),\qquad AD+PC=(AU+DK)+(PK+CX),$$
so $AP+CD=AD+PC$, and by the converse of Pitot's theorem the convex quadrilateral $APCD$ has an incircle $\Omega_A$. Similarly $BCDP$ has an incircle $\Omega_B$.

**$E$ lies on $IJ$.** $\omega$ and $\Omega_A$ are both inscribed in the angle $PCD$, giving a positive homothety $\omega\to\Omega_A$ with centre $C$. $\Omega_A$ and $\Omega$ are both inscribed in the angle $DAB$, giving a positive homothety $\Omega_A\to\Omega$ with centre $A$. The composition is the positive homothety $\omega\to\Omega$, whose centre therefore lies on line $AC$. Using $\Omega_B$ (centres $D$ and $B$), it also lies on line $BD$. So this centre is $E$, and $E$ lies on $IJ$.

Therefore $E$, $I$, $F$ all lie on the line $IJ$. ∎

imo-isl-2007-n1.title: Parity, factor, and growth
imo-isl-2007-n1.body:
**Parity.** $7^k-3^n$ is even, so $k^4+n^2$ is even and $k,n$ have the same parity. If both are odd, then $k^4+n^2\equiv2\pmod 4$, while $7^k-3^n\equiv3-3=0\pmod4$, so the divisibility fails. Hence $k=2a$, $n=2b$.

**Factor.** $7^k-3^n=(7^a-3^b)(7^a+3^b)$ and $7^a-3^b$ is even, so $2(7^a+3^b)\mid7^k-3^n$. Also $7^k-3^n\ne0$ divides $k^4+n^2=2(8a^4+2b^2)>0$. Therefore
$$7^a+3^b\le8a^4+2b^2.\qquad(1)$$

**Growth estimates.** $8a^4<7^a$ for $a\ge4$; $2b^2<3^b$ for $b\ge1$; and $2b^2+9\le3^b$ for $b\ge3$. The base cases are $8\cdot4^4=2048<2401=7^4$, $2<3$, $8<9$, $27\le27$. Inductively,
$$8(a+1)^4=8a^4\Big(\tfrac{a+1}{a}\Big)^4<7^a\Big(\tfrac54\Big)^4<7^{a+1},\qquad 2(b+1)^2+9\le(2b^2+9)\Big(\tfrac{b+1}{b}\Big)^2\le3^b\cdot\tfrac{16}{9}<3^{b+1}.$$
So for $a\ge4$, (1) fails. Hence $a\le3$.

- **$a=1$ ($k=2$).** (1) gives $2b^2+1\ge3^b$, so $b\le2$. For $b=1$: $\frac{2^4+2^2}{7^2-3^2}=\frac{20}{40}$, not an integer. For $b=2$: $\frac{2^4+4^2}{7^2-3^4}=\frac{32}{-32}=-1$. So $(k,n)=(2,4)$ works.
- **$a=2$ ($k=4$).** We need $256+4b^2\ge|7^4-3^n|=|49-3^b|(49+3^b)$. The smallest value of $|49-3^b|$ is $22$ (at $b=3$), so $128+2b^2\ge11(49+3^b)$, impossible since $3^b>2b^2$.
- **$a=3$ ($k=6$).** We need $1296+4b^2\ge|343-3^b|(343+3^b)$, and $|343-3^b|\ge100$ (closest powers $243$ and $729$). So $324+b^2\ge25(343+3^b)$, impossible.

**Answer: $(k,n)=(2,4)$.** ∎

imo-isl-2007-n2.title: Take $k=b^2$
imo-isl-2007-n2.body:
Write $b=p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_s^{\alpha_s}$ with distinct primes $p_i$ and $\alpha_i\ge1$. It suffices to show $n\mid\alpha_i$ for every $i$; then $A=p_1^{\alpha_1/n}\cdots p_s^{\alpha_s/n}$ works.

Apply the hypothesis with $k=b^2>1$ and let $a=a_k$. Then $b^2\mid b-a^n$, so for each $i$, $p_i^{2\alpha_i}\mid b-a^n$, and in particular $p_i^{\alpha_i+1}\mid b-a^n$ (as $2\alpha_i\ge\alpha_i+1$). Since $p_i^{\alpha_i}\mid b$ and $p_i^{\alpha_i+1}\nmid b$,
$$a^n\equiv b\equiv0\pmod{p_i^{\alpha_i}},\qquad a^n\equiv b\not\equiv0\pmod{p_i^{\alpha_i+1}}.$$
So the exact power of $p_i$ dividing $a^n$ is $p_i^{\alpha_i}$. But the exponent of $p_i$ in an $n$-th power is $n$ times its exponent in $a$, so $n\mid\alpha_i$. ∎

*Remark.* Prime values of $k$ alone are not enough: for $b=16$, $n=8$, the congruence $x^8\equiv16\pmod p$ is solvable for every prime $p$, as $x^8-16=(x^2-2)(x^2+2)\big((x+1)^2+1\big)\big((x-1)^2+1\big)$.

imo-isl-2007-n3.title: A good set of residues and averaging
imo-isl-2007-n3.body:
Call a set $M$ of integers *good* if $47\nmid a-b+c-d+e$ for all $a,b,c,d,e\in M$ (not necessarily distinct).

**A good set.** Let $J=\{-9,-7,-5,-3,-1,1,3,5,7,9\}$. For $a,b,c,d,e\in J$ the number $a-b+c-d+e$ is odd (a sum of five odd numbers) and lies between $-45$ and $45$. The only multiple of $47$ in that range is $0$, which is even. So $J$ is good. Its ten elements are pairwise incongruent and nonzero mod $47$.

**Dilations.** For $k=1,\dots,46$ let
$$A_k=\{x\in X:\ kx\equiv j\pmod{47}\text{ for some } j\in J\}.$$
Each $A_k$ is good: if $47\mid a-b+c-d+e$ with $a,\dots,e\in A_k$, then $47\mid ka-kb+kc-kd+ke$, and replacing each term by the congruent element of $J$ gives a violation of goodness for $J$.

**Counting.** Fix $x\in X$. Since $47\nmid x$, for each $j\in J$ there is exactly one $k\in\{1,\dots,46\}$ with $kx\equiv j$ ($k\equiv jx^{-1}$, nonzero because $j\not\equiv0$), and different $j$ give different $k$. So $x$ lies in exactly $10$ of the sets $A_k$, and
$$\sum_{k=1}^{46}|A_k|=10\cdot10\,000=100\,000.$$
Hence some $k$ has $|A_k|\ge\frac{100\,000}{46}>2173>2007$. Any $2007$-element subset $Y$ of this $A_k$ is good, since subsets of good sets are good. ∎

imo-isl-2007-n4.title: Double factorials and an odd polynomial
imo-isl-2007-n4.body:
Write $(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)$; then $(2m)!=2^m\,m!\,(2m-1)!!$, and $v_2$ denotes the exponent of $2$ (extended to rationals).

**Rewriting.** For a positive integer $m$,
$$\binom{4m}{2m}=\frac{(4m)!}{(2m)!^2}=\frac{2^{2m}(2m)!\,(4m-1)!!}{(2m)!^2}=\frac{2^{2m}(4m-1)!!}{(2m)!},\qquad \binom{2m}{m}=\frac{2^m(2m-1)!!}{m!}=\frac{2^{2m}(2m-1)!!^2}{(2m)!},$$
using $m!=\frac{(2m)!}{2^m(2m-1)!!}$. With $m=2^{k-1}$ and $N=2^k$:
$$\binom{2^{k+1}}{2^k}-\binom{2^k}{2^{k-1}}=\frac{2^{N}(N-1)!!}{N!}\Big[(N+1)(N+3)\cdots(2N-1)-(N-1)(N-3)\cdots1\Big]=\frac{2^{N}(N-1)!!}{N!}\,P(N),$$
where
$$P(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(x+2i-1)-\prod_{i=1}^{m}(x-2i+1).$$

**The first factor.** By Legendre's formula $v_2(N!)=2^{k-1}+\dots+2+1=N-1$, and $(N-1)!!$ is odd, so the first factor has $v_2$ equal to $N-(N-1)=1$.

**The polynomial.** Since $m=2^{k-1}$ is even ($k\ge2$), $\prod(x-2i+1)=\prod(-x+2i-1)$, so $P(x)=F(x)-F(-x)$ with $F(x)=\prod(x+2i-1)$. Thus $P$ is an odd polynomial with integer coefficients: $P(x)=x^3Q(x)+cx$ with $Q\in\mathbb Z[x]$, and
$$c=2(N-1)!!\sum_{i=1}^m\frac1{2i-1}.$$
Pairing $2i-1$ with $N-(2i-1)$:
$$c=(N-1)!!\sum_{i=1}^m\Big(\frac1{2i-1}+\frac1{N-2i+1}\Big)=N\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{(N-1)!!}{(2i-1)(N-2i+1)}=N\cdot S.$$
The numbers $2i-1$ and $N-2i+1$ are distinct odd numbers below $N$ (they cannot be equal, as $4i=N+2$ is impossible), so every summand of $S$ is an integer.

**$v_2(S)=k-1$.** Modulo $N$, $N-2i+1\equiv-(2i-1)$. So if $b_i$ is the inverse of $2i-1$ mod $N$, each summand is $\equiv-(N-1)!!\,b_i^2$. As $2i-1$ runs over all odd residues mod $N$, so does $b_i$, hence
$$S\equiv-(N-1)!!\sum_{i=1}^m(2i-1)^2=-(N-1)!!\cdot\frac{m(4m^2-1)}{3}=-(N-1)!!\cdot2^{k-1}\cdot\frac{2^{2k}-1}{3}\pmod{2^k}.$$
The factors $(N-1)!!$ and $\frac{2^{2k}-1}{3}$ are odd, so $S\equiv2^{k-1}\cdot(\text{odd})\pmod{2^k}$, i.e. $v_2(S)=k-1$. Hence $c=2^kS=2^{2k-1}(2t+1)$ for some integer $t$.

**Conclusion.**
$$P(2^k)=2^{3k}Q(2^k)+2^k c=2^{3k}Q(2^k)+2^{3k-1}(2t+1),$$
so $v_2\big(P(2^k)\big)=3k-1$. Therefore the given difference has $v_2$ exactly $1+(3k-1)=3k$: it is divisible by $2^{3k}$ but not by $2^{3k+1}$. (Check for $k=2$: $\binom84-\binom42=64=2^6$.) ∎

imo-isl-2007-n5.title: Residues are preserved
imo-isl-2007-n5.body:
**Lemma.** For every prime $p$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb N$: $x\equiv y\pmod p\iff f(x)\equiv f(y)\pmod p$, and $p\mid f(x)\iff p\mid x$.

*Proof.* Fix $p$. By surjectivity some $f(x)$ is divisible by $p$; let $d$ be the least such $x$.

*Multiples of $d$.* By induction $p\mid f(jd)$ for all $j\ge1$: if $p\mid f(jd)$ and $p\mid f(d)$, then $p\mid f(jd)+f(d)$, so $p\mid f(jd+d)$.

*Only multiples of $d$.* Suppose some $x$ with $d\nmid x$ has $p\mid f(x)$, and let $y$ be the least one. Then $y>d$ and $y-d$ is not divisible by $d$, so by minimality $p\nmid f(y-d)$. But $p\mid f(d+(y-d))$ implies $p\mid f(d)+f(y-d)$, so $p\mid f(y-d)$, a contradiction. Thus
$$p\mid f(x)\iff d\mid x.\qquad(1)$$

*Residues.* Let $x,y\in\mathbb N$ and put $z=2xd-x\in\mathbb N$. Since $d\mid x+z$, (1) gives $p\mid f(x+z)$, hence $p\mid f(x)+f(z)$.
- If $x\equiv y\pmod d$, then $d\mid y+z$, so $p\mid f(y)+f(z)$; subtracting, $f(x)\equiv f(y)\pmod p$.
- If $f(x)\equiv f(y)\pmod p$, then $p\mid f(y)+f(z)$, so $p\mid f(y+z)$, so $d\mid y+z$ by (1), i.e. $d\mid y-x$.

So $x\equiv y\pmod d\iff f(x)\equiv f(y)\pmod p$. (2)

*$d=p$.* The numbers $1,\dots,d$ are distinct mod $d$, so by (2) $f(1),\dots,f(d)$ are distinct mod $p$, giving $d\le p$. By surjectivity pick $x_i$ with $f(x_i)=i$ for $i=1,\dots,p$; these values are distinct mod $p$, so the $x_i$ are distinct mod $d$, giving $p\le d$. With $d=p$, (1) and (2) are the claims. $\square$

**$f(n)=n$ by induction.** No prime divides $1$, so no prime divides $f(1)$, i.e. $f(1)=1$. Let $n>1$, assume $f(j)=j$ for $j<n$, and let $k=f(n)$. A prime factor of $n$ divides $k$, so $k>1$.
- If $k>n$: take a prime $p\mid k-n+1$ (note $k-n+1\ge2$). Then $f(n)=k\equiv n-1=f(n-1)\pmod p$, so by the Lemma $n\equiv n-1\pmod p$, which is impossible.
- If $k<n$: then $f(k-1)=k-1$ (note $k-1\ge1$). Take a prime $p\mid n-k+1\ge2$; then $n\equiv k-1\pmod p$, so by the Lemma $k=f(n)\equiv f(k-1)=k-1\pmod p$, which is impossible.

Hence $f(n)=n$. Conversely the identity is surjective and satisfies the condition trivially, since $f(m+n)=f(m)+f(n)$. **Answer: $f(n)=n$.** ∎

imo-isl-2007-n6.title: Descent on bad pairs
imo-isl-2007-n6.body:
**Lemma.** For positive integers $x,y$: $4xy-1\mid(4x^2-1)^2$ if and only if $x=y$.

If $x=y$ this is clear. Call a pair $(x,y)$ of positive integers *bad* if $4xy-1\mid(4x^2-1)^2$ but $x\ne y$.

*Property (i): if $(x,y)$ is bad and $x<y$, there is a bad pair $(x,z)$ with $z<x$.* Let $r=\frac{(4x^2-1)^2}{4xy-1}$, a positive integer. Modulo $4x$ we have $4xy-1\equiv-1$ and $(4x^2-1)^2\equiv1$, so $-r\equiv1$, i.e. $r\equiv-1\pmod{4x}$. Hence $r=4xz-1$ for some positive integer $z$. As $x<y$, $4xy-1>4x^2-1$, so
$$4xz-1=\frac{(4x^2-1)^2}{4xy-1}<4x^2-1,$$
which gives $z<x$. Since $4xz-1$ divides $(4x^2-1)^2$ (with cofactor $4xy-1$), $(x,z)$ is bad.

*Property (ii): if $(x,y)$ is bad, so is $(y,x)$.* Modulo $4xy-1$ we have $4xy\equiv1$, so
$$(4y^2-1)^2\equiv\big(4y^2-(4xy)^2\big)^2=16y^4(4x^2-1)^2\equiv0\pmod{4xy-1}.$$

*Descent.* Suppose bad pairs exist and choose one with $2x+y$ minimal. If $x<y$, property (i) gives a bad pair $(x,z)$ with $2x+z<2x+y$. If $y<x$, property (ii) gives the bad pair $(y,x)$ with $2y+x<2x+y$. Both contradict minimality, so there are no bad pairs. $\square$

**The problem.** A positive divisor of the form $8kn-1$ needs $n\ge1$, and $8kn-1=4\cdot k\cdot(2n)-1$. By the Lemma with $x=k$, $y=2n$, it divides $(4k^2-1)^2$ if and only if $k=2n$. So such a divisor exists exactly when $k$ is even (then $n=k/2$ works, giving the divisor $4k^2-1$), and never when $k$ is odd. ∎

imo-isl-2007-n7.title: Additivity on a fast-growing sequence
imo-isl-2007-n7.body:
Let $\operatorname{ord}_p(m)$ be the exponent of $p$ in $m$, so $\nu_p(n)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{ord}_p(i)$.

**Lemma.** Let $p$ be prime, $K\ge1$, $N$ a positive multiple of $p^K$, and $0<r<p^K$. Then $\nu_p(N+r)=\nu_p(N)+\nu_p(r)$.

*Proof.* For $0<i<p^K$ let $e=\operatorname{ord}_p(i)<K$. Then $p^e$ divides $N+i$, while $p^{e+1}$ divides $N$ but not $i$; so $\operatorname{ord}_p(N+i)=\operatorname{ord}_p(i)$. Hence
$$\nu_p(N+r)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\operatorname{ord}_p(i)+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{ord}_p(N+i)=\nu_p(N)+\nu_p(r).\ \square$$

**A fast-growing sequence.** Let $P=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$, $n_1=1$, $n_{\ell+1}=P^{n_\ell}$; this sequence is strictly increasing. Let $f(n)=\big(\nu_{p_1}(n),\dots,\nu_{p_k}(n)\big)$.

*Claim:* for $\ell_1<\ell_2<\dots<\ell_m$, $f(n_{\ell_1}+\dots+n_{\ell_m})=f(n_{\ell_1})+\dots+f(n_{\ell_m})$.

Induction on $m$; $m=1$ is trivial. For $m>1$, each $n_{\ell_j}$ with $j\ge2$ equals $P^{n_{\ell_j-1}}$ with $n_{\ell_j-1}\ge n_{\ell_1}$, so $p_i^{n_{\ell_1}}$ divides $N=n_{\ell_2}+\dots+n_{\ell_m}$; also $p_i^{n_{\ell_1}}\ge2^{n_{\ell_1}}>n_{\ell_1}$. The Lemma with $K=n_{\ell_1}$, $r=n_{\ell_1}$ gives $\nu_{p_i}(n_{\ell_1}+N)=\nu_{p_i}(n_{\ell_1})+\nu_{p_i}(N)$ for each $i$, and the induction hypothesis finishes the claim.

**Pigeonhole.** Reduce $f(n_\ell)$ componentwise modulo $d$: there are at most $d^k$ possibilities, so there is an infinite sequence $\ell_1<\ell_2<\dots$ for which all $f(n_{\ell_j})$ are congruent mod $d$ to the same vector $v$. For each $s\ge0$ let
$$N_s=n_{\ell_{sd+1}}+n_{\ell_{sd+2}}+\dots+n_{\ell_{sd+d}}.$$
By the claim, $f(N_s)\equiv d\cdot v\equiv(0,\dots,0)\pmod d$, i.e. $d\mid\nu_{p_i}(N_s)$ for all $i$. The numbers $N_s$ are strictly increasing in $s$, so there are infinitely many such $n$. ∎
